analysis.one_liner: Sets federal safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials, including two-person crews and trackside defect detectors.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill has sat in a House Transportation subcommittee since February 2025 with no vote or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2023 derailment in East Palestine, Ohio released hazardous chemicals into a town, this bill would require trains carrying hazardous materials to meet new federal safety rules: advance notice to state emergency officials, limits on trains blocking road crossings, trackside detectors every 10 miles to catch overheated wheel bearings, at least two crew members on freight trains, safer tank cars phased in by 2027, and fines for safety violations roughly ten times higher than today. Large railroads would pay a $1 million annual fee to fund first-responder training.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along freight rail lines, especially in towns where trains carrying hazardous chemicals pass through road crossings. First responders get better training and advance information about what chemicals are moving through their communities, and rail workers get a two-person crew requirement.

how_it_helps.text: Requires shippers and railroads to give state and Tribal emergency-response officials advance notice and written gas discharge plans for hazardous materials shipments, so local responders know what is coming through [S2].

Directs the Transportation Department to require hotbox detectors — trackside sensors that catch overheated wheel bearings before they cause derailments — every 10 miles on track used by trains carrying hazardous materials, and to set rules for how railroads must respond to alerts [S3].
Writes into law a minimum two-person crew for freight trains, with no exception for trains hauling toxic-by-inhalation materials or long blocks of tank cars [S3].
Phases out older DOT-111 tank cars, the type involved in several major derailment fires, from carrying flammable liquids starting May 1, 2027 [S3].

Raises maximum civil penalties for rail safety violations from as low as $25,000–$175,000 to the greater of $250,000–$1,750,000 or a percentage of the railroad's income, and charges each Class I railroad a $1 million annual fee to fund first-responder hazmat training [S3].
Requires railroads to reduce or eliminate blocked road crossings, a daily hazard and inconvenience in small towns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads — companies like Union Pacific, BNSF, Norfolk Southern, and CSX — would bear the cost of installing detectors every 10 miles, higher fines, a $1 million annual fee, and safer tank cars. Some of those costs would likely flow through to shipping customers and, eventually, to prices for goods moved by rail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large freight railroads and their customers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on the railroads, which would likely pass some of them on through higher freight rates to shippers and consumers [S3].

The blanket two-person crew mandate applies regardless of whether automated inspection technology can perform some of the same safety functions; the bill acknowledges these pilot programs but keeps the crew floor [S3].

Requiring a hotbox detector every 10 miles of track is a heavy capital requirement, and critics of such mandates argue placement rules written in statute can be costlier than risk-based placement chosen by engineers [S3].
The crew-size requirement exempts small short-line railroads with under $40 million in revenue, meaning crews on many local lines would not get the same protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains are concrete: wayside detectors specifically address the wheel-bearing failure that caused the East Palestine derailment, and advance chemical notifications address the emergency-response confusion that followed it. The costs are real but modest relative to Class I railroad revenues, and the bill exempts small railroads from the crew mandate. The main honest criticism is that some mandates (fixed detector spacing, a flat two-person rule) are less flexible than performance-based regulation, so some cost may buy less safety than targeted spending would.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2025 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to two House committees, then sent to the Railroads subcommittee, where it has sat without a markup or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Deluzio introduced the Railway Safety Act of 2025 on February 4, 2025, joined by Reps. LaLota, Rulli, and Garamendi as original sponsors [S1].

The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, and then to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee [S5].
Eleven members have cosponsored it — 5 Democrats and 6 Republicans — giving it support from both parties [S4].
Since the February 2025 referrals, no further action has been taken: no committee vote, no floor vote, in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large freight railroads benefit from the inaction: none of the detector, crew, fine, or fee requirements have taken effect. Communities along rail lines get no new protections.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors split evenly across parties — 5 Democrats and 6 Republicans — and the bill's four original sponsors include two from each party, but no vote has occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill mandates hotbox detectors every 10 miles, two-person crews, roughly tenfold higher safety fines, a $1 million annual fee, and stricter inspections — all costs to the big railroads. Their interest in avoiding these requirements runs directly against the safety protections ordinary people would gain.

industries.industry: Tank car owners and shippers of flammable liquids
industries.note: They would have to retire non-compliant DOT-111 tank cars from flammable-liquid service by May 1, 2027, a costly fleet turnover whose benefit is fewer derailment fires in populated areas.
The statutory two-person crew requirement protects conductor and engineer jobs that railroads have sought to cut through one-person operations, and adds inspection-work protections.

industries.industry: First responders and emergency training programs
industries.note: A $1 million annual fee on each Class I railroad funds hazmat training grants, and supplemental training grants double to $4 million per year.

industries.industry: Trackside detection and rail equipment manufacturers
industries.note: Mandated detector installation every 10 miles and a $22 million grant program create demand for wayside detection equipment and safer tank car technology.

analysis.trajectory: With bipartisan cosponsorship but no committee action since February 2025, the bill's fate rests on the Transportation and Infrastructure chair scheduling a markup, which has not happened. A comparable Railway Safety Act in the previous Congress cleared a Senate committee but never got a full Senate vote, and transportation committees in a divided Congress have prioritized other items. Absent a high-profile new derailment forcing action, the likely path is the bill sitting in subcommittee until this Congress ends.
